title: New guy! Is it worth it??

posts.author: Agate
posts.body:
Hey just discovered RPG Maker MV and debating if I should make this my new hobby/New Years resolution. I say hobby but I really want to put my all into this since I feel like creating a game instead of playing one. I'm wondering if this is sometihng anybody can get into(me with no experience or knowledge) or more for people that know what there doing?(people that went to school or already had prior knowlegde)
- Are tutorials enough? currently watching "SomeRanDev" on YT. Any recommendations?
- Commissions cost? What's the average people spend on original assest? Or I guess how much do you charge for it?
- Artists? Anyone or anywhere to look for people to hire?
- What kind of games have people made with this engine? Is there a place for games other people made? I wanna see whats possible

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body:
Welcome to the forum!
Remember. You don’t have to 0-to-60 it. It’s not overnight that one must decide how deeply to involve themselves into any activity or pursuit. In fact, starting out with small, low scope projects is recommended to get experience and practice.
As to the questions:
RPG Maker is great for beginners because there’s a lot provided up front that can help many over the barrier to entry. You can
absolutely
make a game with what is provided. That said, projects commonly require plugins and other assets that may necessitate a little bit of study to master.
Tutorials and
practice.
Reading any documentation too. Whether written or video, however you learn best should be followed up with applying what you’ve learned. Applied learning is absolutely enough to get the core features of the engine situated.
Original commission costs are going to vary widely depending on what the commissioned item is, how complex it is, what it needs to be compatible with, or if it’s completely original.
It’s difficult to give an umbrella estimate, but many in the RPG Maker community offer very reasonable prices (sometimes too reasonable, IMO). It’s worth considering that even low-end of the price averages will add up. For someone’s
first
project, I’d recommend a project scope utilizing available DLCs, free additions, and if
absolutely needed
a sparing amount of commission work.
I’d also recommend using placeholders until you’re at the point of cementing exactly what you need. It’s common for newer devs to buy and commission a lot early on in development just to realize they want to change something or axe something mid-development.
People can get commissions in a variety of places. There are web services like fiverr that are designed for that purpose. We also do have a commission board here for those looking to stay within the RM community itself,
but new accounts need to meet certain requirements to access it.
If you’d like to check out the games people have made, then head on over to the
projects board
where you’ll find both completed games and games in development.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
RPG Maker markets itself quite literally as THE tool to make games with when you have no clue.
That being said, don't go in thinking you're going to make the next Dragon Quest, Final Fantasy or Pokemon.
It's much better to start small. And I mean very small. Do the provided in-engine tutorial series, and then start making little things. Don't go making that 20 hour, 15 ending rpg. It's not gonna work.
Even if RPG Maker makes it fairly easy to make a game, making one still requires a lot of work, time and learning.

Click to expand...
Anyone can get into it, but I suggest having this in your head - the fact that you're going into this without having the education that people working for software companies normally do means you're going to have to be able to learn to do whatever it is you want to implement.
I don't mean that you need to be able to produce the artwork and coding and music all yourself, but I do mean that you need to be capable of looking things up, reading documentation, experimenting, and troubleshooting.
Asking questions here can help, but you need to have a good dose of self-guided learner in yourself if you have any hope of producing something decent.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Agate said:
Hey just discovered RPG Maker MV and debating if I should make this my new hobby/New Years resolution. I say hobby but I really want to put my all into this since I feel like creating a game instead of playing one.
Click to expand...
Welcome!
Agate said:
I'm wondering if this is sometihng anybody can get into(me with no experience or knowledge) or more for people that know what there doing?(people that went to school or already had prior knowlegde)
Click to expand...
Yes and no.  Let me clarify:
Yes, anyone can get into regardless of experience.  No, not anyone can get into it because it is always more work than you imagine it would be (game making is a lot of work and testing and retesting, and learning).  There are a lot of people who quit gamedev once they realize they can't splurt out a best selling game in less than a year or two of near constant work.
For perspective, I have created over 200 animations in the Database.  They are as low effort as possible (because my brain isn't wired well for making animations for visual art, and it's so tedious).  This was roughly 66 hours (18-20 minutes an animation).  This is JUST the animations for the skills the PLAYER has access to.  I had 4 hours each weekday to work on it and about 6-10 on weekend days (so, about 30 hours a week).  Yeah, took me over 2 weeks to do that.
This is a time sucking hobby.  You'll want to accept that up front.
Agate said:
- Are tutorials enough? currently watching "SomeRanDev" on YT. Any recommendations?
Click to expand...
I'd say "yes and no" to this as well.  Most tutorials will give you "the basics", but not teach you enough to be "useful" with what it is you're learning.
To be more exact, the tutorials will teach you what everything is and how it works, but not necessarily all the "use case" stuff you need to know.
You'll learn how it works mechanically, but not from a "critical thinking" perspective.  As an example, most tutorials will only tell you how the "variable" stuff works by "designing a puzzle". Thus, they only teach you that the variable is good for something like a puzzle.  But, the reality is that you can use variables to randomlize loot in a chest, create a banking system in the game, create a teleport system, manage enemy actions in combat, create an in-game timer for "total playtime", manage cutscenes, manage player choices, and a whole host of other stuff.  "Making a Puzzle" is the least interesting and useful thing you can do with Variables.
Otherwise, most tutorials are "you want to do this one very specific thing for your game?  Here's how!".
Agate said:
- Commissions cost? What's the average people spend on original assest? Or I guess how much do you charge for it?
Click to expand...
I wouldn't worry about this, just starting out.  This is what we call "a newbie trap".
Here's how a pro would do it:
Everything you use in the game is "placeholder".  Keep a running list of assets you want/need as you design the game.  You will cross those assets off the list as you keep making the game and add new ones.
During your GameDev cycle, save a specific amount of money every single week for those future assets you want.  I stick with $5 a week ($5 a week, every week, for 10 years, you can imagine what my budget for assets is!) as my budget.  You can do more or less.  Then, when your game is 100% done, and ready to either be sold or given away for free, you enter the "Polish" cycle.  During "Polish", you take your budget, and start shopping for assets to replace everything that needs replaced.
If you pick up assets early in the cycle, you are doing nothing except shooting yourself in the foot.  You are spending money you don't need to spend, most likely on stuff you won't be using.  The vision for your game will change over time, so there is no sense in getting those assets when you aren't yet done making your game.
Focus on making your game first.  Is it fun, is it done?  If yest to both, then worry about "art assets".  Everything is replaceable at the end of creation of your game.  Do it when you're done.
As for prices... they vary.  Most people are up front about costs of whatever they're offering.  If they aren't, they might price "per job", which means you need to inquire what they'd charge you.
Most artists are also up for "price negotiation" as well.  If they're very kind and you're very good at haggling, you can sometimes get up to a 20% discount on whatever it is you want.  But, most are willing to drop 5% off their prices so long as you're not entitled or a jerk about what you need and when you need it.  Do keep in mind, however, if an artist tells you "prices aren't negotiable", just accept that.  Sometimes, you're a small fish in that pond and they have people willing to pay what you aren't just lining up.  Being a jerk to artists is a fast track to getting ostracized out of that community.
Agate said:
- Artists? Anyone or anywhere to look for people to hire?
Click to expand...
I'm not sure about anywhere else (I'm still in dev cycle), but I know there are some amazing artists on these forums.  You might be able to google for artists if you aren't happy with the quality/prices found here.
Agate said:
- What kind of games have people made with this engine? Is there a place for games other people made? I wanna see whats possible
Click to expand...
The only game that I can think of off the top of my head might be "To The Moon".  But, if you have Steam, there is a tag for "RPG Maker".  You can search that and generally get a very large list of games made in the engine that you could look through the store pages of.  Usually, the videos and images on the store pages are enough to get a feel for "what is possible" in RPG Maker.  No purchase or playing necessary.
However, generally speaking, "what is possible" is going to depend on two factors:
1.  How skilled you are with the engine and what you can imagine doing in it.  There's a lot of stuff people will commission plugins for that actually can be done in engine without them.
2.  If there's a plugin for it.
But, the basic stuff you can make with RPG Maker is probably best classified as "If it could be done on the SNES or Sega Genesis console RPG's, it can be done here".

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
Agate said:
I'm sensing you have some experience with this lol
Click to expand...
Many of us do, myself included. It's not impossible to make your dream game as your first project, but chances are you're getting better as you go and now all your early stuff is kinda jank compared to later content of the game, so now you have to go back and remake the early bits, because you don't want the most important part of your game that will decide whether or not your player sticks around be anything other than ideal.
So in general, it's just better to hone your skills to a certain level in order to make consistent quality content for your game.

posts.author: Indinera

Once I started dumping cash into the project, I decided I wanted the game to be a commercial game, but to be a commercial game I wanted to make sure I hit a certain quality bar with it, and that quality bar has required scope to expand due to design iteration, iteration, iteration; and of course "polishing" scope as referred to by SG.

posts.author: Iron_Brew
posts.body:
Well said!
Most important thing I always try and get people to do is to manage their scope carefully! It's all very well and good having contacts and teams on hand to help out with assets, but knowing what those assets are and what you're gonna need is the best way to keep costs low, or at the very least manageable.
I'd recommend joining a jam or something as a first outing - something with a small scope that lets you use low-cost or free assets (or even the RTP) to go through the process of making (and crucially shipping) a finished miniature game!
There's no better tool in a dev's arsenal than resiliency and experience, so not starting out on your "big" project and in stead getting to grips with the tools and the process of getting something out the door (as well as interacting with feedback and distribution) can really help! Especially in avoiding re-work to get your product to a consistent level of quality in a "big" project as you get more familiar with the tools
